background_notes.fact: For x∈[0,∞] with x<∞, x.toReal≥0 and ofReal(x.toReal)=x. For nonnegative real r,t, ofReal r is finite, ofReal preserves and reflects ≤ and < on r,t, and ofReal(r+t)=ofReal r+ofReal t. If x≤ofReal r for a finite nonnegative real r, then x<∞. Also 0≠∞ and ∞≤x forces x=∞. These facts justify the finite-real identifications in S001, S004, S007 and S010 and the extended-order uses in S003 and S006.

background_notes.justification: The extended nonnegative reals consist of finite nonnegative real values and an additional greatest element ∞. The finite part has exactly the real order and addition. toReal returns that finite value, and ofReal embeds a nonnegative real as that value. A finite element lies strictly below ∞, so an element bounded by it cannot be ∞. The stated identities and order comparisons follow directly in this finite part; the top-element assertions follow from the extended order. All real arguments compared or added in these uses are nonnegative as shown in the argument.

background_notes.fact: A real normed space and ℝ carry their norm metrics. The max metric on their product is a metric, and each of these spaces can be equipped with the Borel σ-algebra generated by its metric open sets. Its associated extended distance is ofReal of its finite metric distance; consequently preservation of metric distances implies preservation of extended distances. Thus all spaces used in A001–A006 admit the required metric/extended metric and Borel structures, and the distance computation in S008 proves the isometry required by M007.

background_notes.justification: The norm axioms give the metric dist(x,y)=||x−y||. For the max product, separation and symmetry follow coordinatewise; its triangle inequality follows from each coordinate triangle inequality and max(a+c,b+d)≤max(a,b)+max(c,d) for nonnegative a,b,c,d. The σ-algebra generated by open sets is the Borel measurable structure by construction. Embedding finite distances in [0,∞] preserves equality and the metric inequalities. In S008 the first coordinate is constant, so its distance is zero and max(0,|t−u|)=|t−u|, proving the required distance preservation without any property of x0 beyond being a point of V.
